text: # Hip Osteoarthritis: Clinical Overview ## Description Osteoarthritis represents a degenerative joint condition affecting individuals primarily over age 50, though younger people may develop it. The disorder involves gradual deterioration of cartilage that normally cushions the hip joint. As this protective tissue wears away, bones may rub together, and damaged areas can develop bone spurs to compensate for lost cartilage. ## Causes & Risk Factors The condition lacks a single definitive cause but occurs more frequently in individuals with: - Advanced age - Family history of the disease - Prior hip joint injuries - Excess body weight - Congenital hip malformation (developmental dysplasia) Development remains possible without these risk factors. ## Symptoms Pain represents the primary symptom, typically developing gradually and intensifying over time. Patients commonly experience: - Groin or thigh discomfort radiating toward buttocks or knee - Morning stiffness or post-activity soreness - Joint "locking" or grinding sensations

text: # Hip Bursitis: Comprehensive Overview ## What Are Bursae? Bursae are small, jelly-like sacs that are located throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. These structures contain fluid and function as cushions between bones and soft tissues, reducing friction during movement. ## Types of Hip Bursitis Two major bursae in the hip can become inflamed: 1. **Trochanteric bursitis**: Affects the bursa covering the greater trochanter (bony hip point), causing lateral hip pain 2. **Iliopsoas bursitis**: Involves the bursa on the groin side of the hip, less common but treated similarly ## Symptoms Patients typically experience sharp, intense pain at the hip point that may extend to the outer thigh. Early-stage symptoms intensify at night, when lying on the affected side, and when rising from seated positions.

text: # Carpal Tunnel Syndrome ## Description & Anatomy Carpal tunnel syndrome is a common condition that causes numbness, tingling, and pain in the hand and forearm. The condition develops when one of the major nerves to the hand -- the median nerve -- is squeezed or compressed as it travels through the wrist. The carpal tunnel itself is a narrow passageway in the wrist, about an inch wide, with floors and sides formed by small wrist bones. The roof of the tunnel is a strong band of connective tissue called the transverse carpal ligament. Because these boundaries are rigid, the carpal tunnel has little capacity to stretch or increase in size. The median nerve originates as a group of nerve roots in the neck and travels down the upper arm, across the elbow, and into the forearm, then passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist on its way to the hand and fingers.

source_note: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS) - OrthoInfo
text: The median nerve originates as a group of nerve roots in the neck and travels down the upper arm, across the elbow, and into the forearm, then passes through the carpal tunnel at the wrist on its way to the hand and fingers. It provides sensation to the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and half of the ring finger, and controls the muscles around the base of the thumb. Nine flexor tendons also travel through the tunnel, enabling finger and thumb bending. Without treatment, in most patients carpal tunnel syndrome gets worse over time, and can lead to permanent dysfunction of the hand, including loss of sensation in the fingers and weakness. ## Cause Most cases result from a combination of factors. Women and older people show higher incidence rates. Risk factors include: - **Heredity**: The carpal tunnel may be naturally smaller in some people, or there may be anatomic differences that change the amount of space for the nerve, and this can run in families.

This often wakes people up at night.

Types include: - **Nerve conduction studies (NCS)**: These tests measure the signals travelling in the nerves of the hand and arm and can detect when a nerve is not conducting its signal effectively.

Splints may also be worn during aggravating daytime activities. - **Activity changes**: Since symptoms often occur when the hand and wrist are in the same position for too long, modifying activities or workstations can slow or stop progression of the disease. - **Nerve gliding exercises**: Some patients may benefit from exercises that help the median nerve move more freely within the confines of the carpal tunnel. ## Surgical Treatment

The decision considers symptom severity, physical exam findings, response to non-operative treatment, and testing results. In long-standing cases with constant numbness and wasting of the thumb muscles, surgery may be recommended to prevent irreversible damage. ### Surgical Procedure The procedure is called "carpal tunnel release." The goal is to relieve pressure on the median nerve by cutting the ligament that forms the roof of the tunnel (transverse carpal ligament). Release of this ligament increases the size of the tunnel and decreases pressure on the median nerve, allowing for appropriate blood flow to the nerve and function. In most cases, carpal tunnel surgery is done on an outpatient basis.

In most cases, carpal tunnel surgery is done on an outpatient basis. The surgery can be done under general anesthesia, which puts you to sleep, or under local anesthesia, which numbs just the hand and arm. **Open carpal tunnel release**: The surgeon makes a small incision in the palm of the hand and views the inside of the hand and wrist through this incision, then divides the transverse carpal ligament (the roof of the carpal tunnel). This increases the size of the tunnel and decreases pressure on the median nerve. After surgery, the ligament may gradually grow back together in a lengthened fashion, but there will be more space in the carpal tunnel.

Nighttime symptoms improve dramatically for most patients in the first week or so after surgery. **Grip and pinch strength** usually return by about 2 to 3 months after surgery. If the condition of the median nerve was poor before surgery, grip and pinch strength may not improve for about 6 to 12 months. **Numbness and tingling** tend to improve over the first several months after surgery. Some patients with mild disease may experience return of sensation right away. Patients with severe disease may not have normal sensation in their fingertips for 6 to 12 months after surgery. Recovery, however, may be gradual, and complete recovery may take up to a year. If you have significant pain and weakness for more than 2 months, your doctor may refer you to a hand therapist who can help you maximize your recovery. Additional conditions like arthritis or tendinitis may slow recovery. In long-standing cases of carpal tunnel syndrome with severe loss of feeling and/or muscle wasting around the base of the thumb, recovery will also be slower, and for these patients a complete recovery may not be possible.

text: # Low Back Pain Almost every adult will experience low back pain at some point in their lives. Pain severity ranges from mild to severe, and may be temporary or chronic, sometimes accompanied by leg discomfort. ## Key Causes **Overactivity and muscle strain** Repetitive or unfamiliar activities cause muscle and ligament overstretching. text: # Gout: Causes and Treatments ## Overview Gout is characterized by sudden attacks of intense pain, swelling, and redness in the joints or soft tissues. The big toe joints are commonly affected first, though gout can develop in multiple joints. The condition develops when uric acid crystals accumulate in joints and soft tissues, triggering an inflammatory response similar to an infection. ## What Gout Affects Gout impacts several tissue types: - **Joints**: Most commonly the big toe, but also fingers, knees, shoulders, elbows, and hips. - **Bursae**: Fluid-filled sacs that cushion bones and soft tissues, particularly at the elbow and kneecap. - **Tendon sheaths**: Protective tunnels in the hands and feet. - **Kidneys**: Elevated uric acid can cause kidney stones (affecting approximately 15% of gout patients). ## Progression Following the initial attack, subsequent episodes may occur within 2 years for untreated individuals.

Over time, attacks become more frequent and severe, potentially affecting multiple joints simultaneously. Chronic cases can produce chalky deposits called tophi and cause permanent joint damage resembling arthritis. ## Causes and Risk Factors Gout develops when the body produces excessive uric acid or fails to eliminate sufficient quantities. text: # Lumbar Spinal Stenosis Lumbar spinal stenosis is a common cause of low back and leg pain, or sciatica. The condition develops as the spine ages and degenerative changes narrow the spinal canal, compressing the nerves. It most commonly affects adults over 60. ## Causes Arthritis represents the primary cause. As spinal disks lose water content with age, they shrink and collapse. This settling creates two problems: increased pressure on the facet joints (triggering arthritis) and shrinking of the nerve exit tunnels. Degenerating facet joints develop bone spurs, and thickened ligaments further crowd the nerve space. ## Symptoms Common presentations include: - Back pain (variable intensity) - Burning pain in the buttocks or legs (sciatica) - Numbness or tingling sensations - Leg weakness or foot drop - Cauda equina syndrome (a medical emergency involving bowel/bladder dysfunction)

text: - Burning pain in the buttocks or legs (sciatica) - Numbness or tingling sensations - Leg weakness or foot drop - Cauda equina syndrome (a medical emergency involving bowel/bladder dysfunction) Patients typically feel better when leaning forward or sitting; standing and walking worsen the pain. ## Nonsurgical Treatment Options - Physical therapy and core strengthening - Acupuncture and chiropractic manipulation (with caution) - Lumbar traction (limited scientific evidence of benefit) ## Surgical Treatment Two main approaches: **Laminectomy:** Removes bone, spurs, and ligaments compressing the nerves. text: # Cervical Spondylosis: Arthritis of the Neck ## Overview Neck pain frequently stems from age-related changes. Cervical spondylosis, commonly called arthritis of the neck, is the medical term for these age-related, wear-and-tear changes that occur over time. This condition affects over 85% of people older than 60, though many experience no symptoms. ## Anatomy The cervical spine consists of seven vertebrae forming the neck. The spine contains the spinal cord and nerve roots, intervertebral disks (shock absorbers made of an outer annulus fibrosus and soft nucleus pulposus center), and facet joints providing stability. ## Causes Cervical spondylosis results from normal degenerative aging. As disks lose water content and height, they weaken. Increased pressure causes facet joints to deteriorate. Cartilage wearing away can trigger bone spur formation, potentially narrowing the space for nerves (stenosis).

text: # Cervical Spondylosis ## Overview Cervical spondylosis is a prevalent condition affecting individuals over 40, characterized by neck and shoulder pain, often in people over 40. It is the medical term for neck problems caused by age-related "wear and tear" to bones and discs in the neck. ## Symptoms The condition presents with: - Neck and shoulder discomfort or stiffness that fluctuates - Headaches originating at the base of the neck - Many people experience no symptoms at all, as this represents a normal part of aging ## Self-Care Measures Recommended approaches include: - Performing gentle neck exercises - Correcting postural habits ## When to Seek Medical Attention **Non-urgent (see a GP):** Consult a GP if pain persists beyond several weeks or worsens with movement. **Urgent (call NHS 111):** Seek help for severe sudden pain, arm/leg weakness, tingling sensations, or shoulder blade pain.

Treatment involves exercises, maintaining activity levels, and potentially muscle relaxants for chronic pain. Surgery is reserved for nerve compression or spinal cord involvement. ## Causes Age-related wear and tear of spinal bones and discs cause the condition, with increased risk following previous neck injuries or in people with a family history.

text: # Sprains, Strains & Other Soft-Tissue Injuries ## Overview Soft-tissue injuries affect muscles, tendons, and ligaments, and typically occur during sports and exercise. Common examples include sprains, strains, and contusions, as well as tendinitis and bursitis, and even with appropriate treatment these injuries may require a long time to heal. ## Cause: Acute vs. Overuse Injuries Soft-tissue injuries fall into two basic categories: **Acute injuries** are caused by a sudden trauma, such as a fall, twist, or blow to the body. Examples include sprains, strains, and contusions. **Overuse injuries** occur gradually over time when an athletic or other activity is repeated so often that the soft tissues do not have enough time to recover. Tendinitis and bursitis are examples of overuse injuries. ## RICE Protocol for Acute Injuries

Your doctor may recommend that you use crutches to avoid putting weight on an injured leg. - **Ice**: Use cold packs for 20 minutes out of 1 hour, several times a day. Do not apply ice directly to the skin. - **Compression**: To help stop swelling, wear an elastic compression bandage. - **Elevation**: To reduce swelling, elevate the injury higher than your heart while resting. ## Sprains A sprain is a stretch and/or tear of a ligament, a strong band of connective tissue that connects the end of one bone with another. Ligaments stabilize and support the body's joints.

text: ## Sprains A sprain is a stretch and/or tear of a ligament, a strong band of connective tissue that connects the end of one bone with another. Ligaments stabilize and support the body's joints. The most vulnerable areas for sprains are the ankles, knees, and wrists -- for example, ankle sprains from the foot turning inward, knee sprains from a sudden twist, and wrist sprains from a fall onto an outstretched hand. Sprains are classified by severity: - **Grade 1 (mild)**: Slight stretching and some damage to the fibers of the ligament. - **Grade 2 (moderate)**: Partial tearing of the ligament, with abnormal looseness (laxity) in the joint. - **Grade 3 (severe)**: Complete tear of the ligament, causing significant instability. Common symptoms across all grades include pain, bruising, swelling, and inflammation.

Moderate sprains often require bracing (for example, CAM walking boots for ankle sprains, or hinged knee braces). Severe sprains may require surgery to repair torn ligaments. ## Strains A strain is an injury to a muscle and/or tendon. Tendons are fibrous cords of tissue that attach muscles to bone. Common locations for strains include the back, neck, and legs (particularly the hamstring). A strain may involve a simple stretch of a muscle or tendon, or it may involve a partial or complete tear. Symptoms include pain, muscle spasm, muscle weakness, swelling, inflammation, and cramping.

text: **Treatment** is the same as for sprains: rest, ice, compression, and elevation, followed by exercises to relieve pain and restore mobility. Surgery may be needed for severe tears. ## Contusions (Bruises) Contusions occur when a direct blow (or repeated blows) by a blunt object strikes part of the body, crushing underlying muscle fibers and connective tissue without breaking the skin. Discoloration results from blood pooling around the injury. Most contusions respond well to the RICE protocol. Quadriceps contusions specifically benefit from a compression wrap and temporary immobilization of the thigh with the knee in a bent position. Persistent symptoms warrant medical evaluation to prevent permanent damage. ## Tendinitis Tendinitis is an inflammation or irritation of a tendon or the covering of a tendon (called a sheath). It results from a series of small stresses that repeatedly aggravate the tendon, with symptoms of swelling and pain that worsens with activity.

Sports with high risk for tendinitis include overhead sports (baseball, softball, swimming, tennis, volleyball, golf), which affect the shoulders and elbows, and running and jumping sports (soccer, basketball, running, aerobic dancing), which affect the knees and ankles. Persistent inflammation may cause significant damage to the tendon, which may require surgery. ## Bursitis Bursae are small, jelly-like sacs located throughout the body, including around the shoulder, elbow, hip, knee, and heel. They contain fluid and act as cushions to reduce friction. Bursitis results when repeated small stresses and overuse cause the bursa to swell, and it often accompanies tendinitis.

Surgery is rarely needed unless infection occurs; removal may be performed via standard incision (open procedure) or as an arthroscopic procedure with small incisions. ## Prevention Injuries often occur when people suddenly increase the duration, intensity, or frequency of their activities. Many soft-tissue injuries can be prevented through proper conditioning and training. Specific prevention strategies include: - **Equipment**: Replace athletic shoes as they wear out, and wear comfortable, loose-fitting clothes that let you move freely. - **Fitness balance**: Develop a balanced fitness program that incorporates cardiovascular exercise, strength training, and flexibility. Add activities and new exercises cautiously, no more than one or two new activities per workout. - **Warm-up**: Warm up to prepare for exercise, even before stretching.

text: Add activities and new exercises cautiously, no more than one or two new activities per workout. - **Warm-up**: Warm up to prepare for exercise, even before stretching. Warming up increases your heart and blood flow rates and loosens up muscles, tendons, ligaments, and joints. - **Stretching**: Begin stretches slowly and carefully until reaching a point of muscle tension. Hold each stretch for 10 to 20 seconds, then slowly release. Never stretch to the point of pain, always maintain control, and never bounce on a muscle that is fully stretched. - **Hydration**: Drink 1 pint of water 15 minutes before you start exercising and another pint after you cool down. Have a drink of water every 20 minutes or so while you exercise. - **Cool-down**: Make cooling down the final phase of your exercise routine. It should take twice as long as your warm-up, for at least 10 minutes before you stop completely.

text: # Sprains and Strains ## Overview Sprains and strains are common injuries that affect the muscles and ligaments. Most can be treated at home without needing to see a GP. ## Symptoms It's likely to be a sprain or strain if you have pain, tenderness or weakness - usually around your ankle, foot, wrist, thumb, knee, leg or back - along with swelling, bruising, being unable to put weight on the injury or use it normally, and muscle spasms or cramping. ## Sprain vs Strain A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament. Sprains are most common in your wrists, ankles, thumbs and knees. A strain is an overstretched or torn muscle (sometimes called a "pulled" muscle). text: Strains most often happen in your feet, legs or back. ## Self-Treatment: PRICE Therapy For the first 2 to 3 days, follow the five steps known as PRICE: 1. **Protection** - protect the area from further injury, for example by using a support 2. **Rest** - stop exercising and try to avoid putting weight on the injury 3. **Ice** - apply an ice pack (or a bag of frozen peas wrapped in a towel) to the injury for up to 20 minutes every 2 to 3 hours 4. **Compression** - wrap a bandage around the injury to support it 5. **Elevation** - keep it raised on a pillow as much as possible During this time, try to avoid heat (such as hot baths), alcohol, running, or massage, as this may increase swelling. When you can move the injured area without pain stopping you, try to keep moving it so the joint or muscle does not become stiff.

Try not to do any strenuous exercise, such as running, for up to 8 weeks, as there's a risk of further injury. Severe sprains and strains can take months to heal fully. ## When to Get Further Help Call NHS 111 or get help from 111 online if: - the pain or swelling gets worse, or does not start to improve after a few days of treating it at home - you cannot put any weight at all on the injury or you cannot use the affected joint - the area feels stiff and it's hard to move it - you have a very painful lump on the muscle - you have tingling or loss of sensation - the injury has not improved after 2 weeks
